profiles.name: Batsirai Chikukwa
profiles.source: Artist autobiography supplied by House of Mabwe owner, 19 November 2026
profiles.introduction: Batsirai Chikukwa is a Zimbabwean stone sculptor who trained under Chenjerai Chiripanyanga and works across abstract forms and birds.
profiles.biography:
Batsirai Chikukwa was born in Harare, Zimbabwe, in 1984. He attended St. Peter's Private School and continued his secondary education at Goromonzi Boarding School around 2000. In 2003, he met the sculptor Chenjerai Chiripanyanga, whose encouragement led him to begin learning stone carving. Over approximately three years of guidance and practical work, Chikukwa developed the foundations of his craft.

Drawing on that experience, he began forming an artistic approach of his own at Tsindi Gallery. He later joined the ZIMSA artists' association, based along Airport Road in Hatfield, Harare, where he says he continues his practice. His stated areas of interest include abstract forms and birds, subjects that allow him to move between recognisable natural shapes and more open sculptural compositions.

Chikukwa is represented in the House of Mabwe collection by Celebration, a seated drummer carved in stone. The musician's hands, instrument and posture come together in a single figure, giving the work a sense of rhythm and human presence. It offers another view of his ability to translate a familiar moment into sculptural form.

profiles.name: Martin Matimura
profiles.source: House of Mabwe owner confirmed Martin Matimura's passing, 19 November 2026; no death date or circumstances provided
profiles.introduction: The late Martin Matimura is represented in the collection by figurative stone carving that explores connection through two distinct faces held within one form.
profiles.biography:
The late Martin Matimura is represented in the House of Mabwe collection by Paired Reflection, a stone sculpture bringing two faces into a shared composition. Their profiles remain distinct, while a carved structure above them creates a visual connection. The work can suggest the bonds of family, friendship or common experience without asking the viewer to read the two figures as identical.

The composition balances detailed figurative carving with more abstract lines. Grooves across the upper section lead the eye between the faces, while the open space separating their profiles keeps each individual visible. In this work, Matimura left a thoughtful study of closeness and individuality. His sculpture remains part of the collection and a lasting record of his artistry.
